name: Saint Mary's Park
note: Matched as St. Mary's Recreation Center/Playground, Justin Drive near Bernal Heights.

facts.text: The city set aside 13 acres for the recreation area, which Mayor Elmer Robinson dedicated in 1951.
Works Progress Administration crews shaped the hillside land in the 1930s.
Built on three tiers of a steep hill, with a gymnasium, auditorium and baseball diamond on the first.
A rooftop park designed by Robert Royston in 1957 on top of a parking garage.
Has a statue of Sun Yat-sen by Beniamino Bufano, erected in 1937.
Has a memorial plaque to Chinese Americans who died serving in World Wars I and II.
Funded by a bequest from Helene Strybing, and planting began in 1937 with Works Progress Administration money.
Covers 55 acres with nearly 9,000 kinds of plants from around the world.
Was named Strybing Arboretum until 2004.
Has a bust of Shakespeare donated by James D. Phelan, a copy of the bust in Holy Trinity Church, Stratford-upon-Avon.
Plants are flowers mentioned in Shakespeare's works, with six bronze plaques of his quotes about flowers.
Friends of Recreation and Parks renovated it from December 1990 to June 1991.
Also called Lakeview and Ashton Mini Park.
A rocky outcrop on a ridge of sandstone in the Merced and Ingleside Heights neighborhoods.
Native plants on its slopes include buckwheat, dudleya, farewell-to-spring, coast onion and soap plant.
Built in 1979 by the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency as a mini-park for new Hunters Point Hill housing.
Reopened after a $3.3 million renovation with a new play area, picnic area and fitness equipment.
A 33-acre grove donated to the city in 1931 by Rosalie Meyer Stern and named for her husband Sigmund Stern.
Dedicated on June 4, 1932, with landscaping and facilities built by the Works Progress Administration.
Renovated in 2005 in a $15 million project designed by landscape architect Lawrence Halprin.
Has a baseball diamond, athletic field, outdoor basketball court, tennis courts and a children's playground.
Also called South Beach Harbor Park, between Pier 40 and Oracle Park on the Embarcadero.
Has a 42,000 square foot lawn with a large sculpture by artist Mark di Suvero.
Has a children's playground of about 4,000 square feet.
Dedicated in 1984 on land cleared and given by Barratt Construction, developers of Parkview Heights.
A roughly 3.5 acre protected open space between 23rd and Carolina and 24th and De Haro.
Part of a line of serpentine grassland running across San Francisco.
A hill rising 412 feet that forms an island in Blue Heron Lake, formerly Stow Lake, connected by two bridges.
Has Huntington Falls, a 110-foot waterfall named for Collis P. Huntington, who donated $25,000 toward it.
Formerly called Ferry Park, it is a 4.5-acre park named for civic activist and Supervisor Sue Bierman.
Built on the former footprint of the Embarcadero Freeway ramps.
Has a community room, outdoor basketball court, tennis courts, picnic area and playground with a large sandbox.
A two-mile park along the Upper Great Highway from Sloat Boulevard to Lincoln Way.
Features a skate park, a bike pump track and fitness equipment.
Created after voters approved Proposition K in November 2024 to close the Upper Great Highway to cars.
Open to the Sunset community since 1940, on nearly four acres.
Has a gymnasium, baseball field, basketball court, two tennis courts and a table tennis room.
Has paved and unpaved walking paths along the north side of the Sunset Reservoir.

name: Sunset Tunnel Park
note: Only the Sunset Tunnel (Muni) and nearby Duboce Park / Richard Gamble Memorial Park turned up; no source names a park called Sunset Tunnel Park.

facts.text: Created in 1885 by Adolph Sutro as a public garden of over twenty acres, and opened to the public free of charge.
The Sutro family gave it to the city in 1920, and it passed to Golden Gate National Recreation Area in 1976.
Sutro filled the garden with over 200 concrete replicas of Greek and Roman statues imported from Belgium.
A two-acre park designed by Peter Walker as part of the Golden Gateway redevelopment.
Completed in 1966 and named for banker Sydney Grant Walton, a former vice chairman of the Redevelopment Agency.
Holds an arch from the Colombo Market and artworks by Jim Dine, Marisol and Joan Brown.
A 2.9-acre natural area on Twin Peaks Boulevard.
Named for the Clarendon Heights Water Tank, built there in 1894 by the Spring Valley Water Company.
The city bought the hill back for $650,000 after neighbors opposed a housing development.

name: Terrace Green Park
note: Owned by the St. Francis Homes Association for residents and their guests, so not a public city park.

facts.text: Designed by the Olmsted Brothers with lawns, tennis courts and a clubhouse; today has a basketball court and two tennis courts.

name: Topaz Open Space
note: City page confirms Topaz Open Space is managed by SF Rec and Park; little else sourced.

facts.text: Also listed as a birding hotspot called Topaz Open Space/Gold Mine Hill in Diamond Heights.
Designed in 1969 by Thomas Galli and built in 1972 alongside the Transamerica Pyramid.
Planted with 80 mature redwoods from the Santa Cruz Mountains, of which 50 remain.
Has a sunken pool and fountain by Anthony Guzzardo and a bronze sculpture of running children by Glenna Goodacre added in 1989.

name: Tulare Park
note: Only aggregator listings (mypacer, mapcarta) mention a Tulare Park near 1301 Indiana St; no city or news source found.

facts.text: Received the San Francisco Parks Alliance 2016 Innovative Project of the Year award.
Has a labyrinth, murals and a mosaic seating wall.
Has an S.P. Tunnels mural by Eli Lippert and Monica Magtoto based on a 1935 woodcut by Charles Surendorf.
